extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing vivid descriptive prose and realistic, effective dialogue in fiction (short stories and novels). Covers figurative language, sensory detail, point of view, and dialogue conventions and purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fresh, surprising similes and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech should be 'too fresh, too surprising' — not the hackneyed images heard in everyday speech (e.g., avoid 'like a house on fire' when writing fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures of speech reach into the reader's subconscious, pulling up visual images and remembered experiences. Prefer original comparisons that reframe familiar things; test by asking whether the image feels new. Examples given: 'She felt like an object unraveling in every direction.' and 'His gaze penetrated her so thoroughly, it was as though he had thrust his hand into her chest and begun feeling her ribs one by one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose simile vs. metaphor to fit tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors feel more powerful and can lend a heavier narrative style; similes are suppler and more flexible (can be used in dialogue, first-person, headlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the story's tone and narrator when choosing: use similes for elasticity and lightness; use metaphors for weight and sustained effect. Be cautious with extended metaphors — they can push a story toward allegory (e.g., Kafka's The Metamorphosis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ lyricism (sound and rhythm) in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyricism means prose that plays with sound and rhythm like poetry, sinking the story deeper into readers' subconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read your work aloud to hear rhythm, where phrasing 'clunks', and where words 'slide and sing'. Lyricism need not mean long sentences (Hemingway's short sentences can still be musical). Use it to carry nonverbal meaning; listen for chantlike or musical patterns (examples: Joyce, Hemingway).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use onomatopoeia to mimic sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Onomatopoeia uses words that sound like what they represent (e.g., murmur, buzz, hiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle words that mimic sounds to make scenes more immediate and sensory; ensure they fit tone and don't become gimmicky. Example: 'the tea kettle hisses.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alliteration judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Alliteration (repeating initial sounds) can introduce a graceful highlight to description but is easily overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage alliteration as a subtle grace note; avoid excessive repetition that calls attention to technique rather than content. Example: 'His soul swooned slowly... the snow falling faintly...' demonstrates effective use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend multiple devices naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative elements (simile, metaphor, lyricism, alliteration, onomatopoeia, synesthesia) can be combined for an effortless flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for organic blending rather than piling on devices. Read aloud to check balance. Example: Mukherjee's passage mixes alliteration, simile, onomatopoeia and rhythm to good effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use synesthesia (cross-sensory images) to enliven description
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply an image or adjective usually associated with one sense to another (e.g., 'the sound that washed your senses', 'his dark chocolate voice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synesthesia can produce startling, vivid imagery; experiment freely in drafts. Examples: Keats and author’s own examples. Beware of overuse — use for high-impact moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select telling details that capture the essence
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'telling detail' conveys the essence of what it's describing in a compact, memorable way (e.g., Scotch tape holding up Susie's hemline, the tiny piece of ice in Mom's martini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling details act as shorthand that evokes character, place, or atmosphere. Choose one or a few such details to represent the whole rather than cataloguing everything. Examples: a voice, a particular pair of eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading with description — choose details
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a fine line between lush description and detail that 'chokes the reader' and interrupts story flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always ask: Does the description interrupt the flow of the story? Prefer a golden mean: enough detail to paint the picture but not so much that the narrative stalls. If uncertain, be generous in drafting then cut during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous in drafting, then pare to the telling detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Novice writers should put down all sensory detail in early drafts; later identify and retain the telling detail(s) and remove excess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft expansively to discover which details stick; subsequent drafts should compress and refine (the author describes drafts unfolding and compressing across versions). This process prevents under-describing early on and over-describing in final text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and stale phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of overused expressions (e.g., 'bone-chilling cold', 'he smiled daggers', 'sleeping like the dead') because they are meaningless from overuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clichés leave readers unengaged and paint 'almost nothing' in the mind's eye. Markers/clichés can be used temporarily in drafts as placeholders, but revise them into specific, fresh language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise and avoid sloppy or impossible metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure imagery and comparisons are accurate and internally coherent (avoid statements like 'He felt like a punching bag without air').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an image is factually wrong or imprecise it breaks reader belief. Fix by choosing accurate analogues (e.g., 'a balloon without air' or 'a punching bag without stuffing'). Proof for literal accuracy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed or inconsistent metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't combine incompatible metaphors (e.g., having a character 'swim against a tide' and 'climb a tall mountain' in the same sentence or passage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed metaphors confuse spatial/imaginal logic and dilute impact. Keep metaphoric imagery coherent within scenes and across a narrative arc (you can make a character a fish, but don't turn her into an elephant later without reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Render inner life through sensory, specific details
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions and thoughts should be shown via physical sensations, actions, or sensory detail rather than abstract labels ('she was angry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'objective correlative' (T.S. Eliot): name external facts/sensory details that evoke the emotion. Examples: tight chest, flushed skin, jaw tightened, 'Rage closed her throat.' This makes readers feel the emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let POV/filter color description
rubrics_metrics.description: When narration is filtered through a character's consciousness, that subjectivity should shape how things are described (perceptions may not be objectively true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the character's perceptions, biases, and emotional state to render objects and people (e.g., a character's view of someone's hands, hair, or attractiveness). Ensure consistency with POV and that subjective descriptions reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scene (showing) with dialogue for important moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene depicts action in real time (showing) and is where dialogue appears; it's more powerful than summary for key moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save summary for efficiency or when the narrator needs to 'tell.' For moments of real significance (plot turning points, character confrontations), switch to scene and let dialogue show the moment. Example: the hospital scene with the surgeon announcing 'Wilm's tumor' is more powerful in scene form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose when to use dialogue — keep it focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should be used for moments of real significance (character development, plot advancement, drama); avoid long, boring exchanges that inflate unimportant moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dialogue scene doesn't advance plot or deepen character, consider summarizing instead. Avoid giving equal dramatic weight to trivial exchanges; prioritize high-impact interactions for full dialogue scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dialogue sound real but purposeful (the illusion of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should capture realistic speech patterns, but be more focused and consequential than ordinary conversation — fiction requires sharpened, relevant dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to real speech to develop an ear, use contractions and natural rhythms, but edit out the long, aimless parts of real conversation. Transcribe then tighten: keep the flavor of speech but ensure each line conveys character or advances story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use character-appropriate diction and allow cliché in voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may use contractions and even hackneyed phrasing; this can be appropriate if it fits the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractions are generally good for realism. If a character would naturally say a cliché ('hot as hell'), it's acceptable in dialogue even if you would avoid it in descriptive prose. Tailor speech to each character's background and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow dialogue conventions for readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional presentation makes dialogue clear: typically double quotation marks and one paragraph per speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick with standard punctuation (double quotes) unless you have a compelling reason to break convention. Dedicate a paragraph to each speaker, regardless of length, to avoid reader confusion. Alternatives (dashes, single quotes) can be used deliberately but sparingly.
